submission.natural_language_explanation: The positive pole fires on tokens of the elevated, literary-historical stratum of written English: uncommon content words of narrative, history, religion, the arts and formal description - mostly nouns and their Latinate pieces (artillery, mortar, harbour, treasury, refinery, repertoire, alloy, saddle, loaf, abode, ferry, cargo, plague, meteor, venture, leisure, jazz, violin, cavalry, squadron, army, relics, cathedral, grace, brink, muster, sterling, currency) - plus many proper names - brand, place and person names such as Barclays, Sinai, Maine and Adobe. It stays near zero on function words and punctuation, on everyday domestic and modern-institutional vocabulary (kettle, towel, ladder, table, chair, house, kitchen, boat, money, bread, phone, office, committee, database), on the common core of ordinary adjectives and verbs (big, enormous, prodigious, announced, walked), on administrative or technical jargon used in its technical sense (parliament, ministry, legislation, jurisdiction, bureaucracy, software, browser, protocol), and on very obscure bookish words of the same register (frigate, vellum, edict, minstrel, abbey).

In the spring of the year 1704 the town of Vellmar lay under a low grey sky, and the river carried silt past the old wharves. The council had spent the winter arguing about the harbour, whose walls had fallen into ruin, and about the treasury, which could not pay for the repairs. A captain of artillery arrived on the third day, bringing orders from the capital and a chest of maps that nobody could read. He spoke of a squadron wintering beyond the hills, of cavalry promised but never sent, and of a ferry that had sunk with its cargo in the spring floods. The townspeople listened in the square, where the market stalls stood empty and the fountain had frozen.

That evening the priest led a procession to the cathedral, where the relics of the town's patron were kept behind glass, and the choir sang a hymn that no one had rehearsed. Outside, a meteor crossed the sky above the bell tower, and an old woman said it was an omen of plague. The blacksmith, who had spent the week casting a new alloy for the bells, would not look up from his forge.

By the middle of the month the roads were mud and the granaries were low. A merchant from the coast offered sterling for the last of the wool, but the council refused, saying the price was an insult to the town. The merchant shrugged and rode away, and the children ran after his cart until the gate closed behind him. The miller ground the last of the rye and sold the flour at a price the poor could not pay, and two families left for the coast before the roads closed. In the churchyard the sexton dug a grave for a beggar who had died of the cold, and the bell rang once, briefly, as if ashamed.

The chronicler of Vellmar, who kept his notes in a leather book, wrote that nothing of consequence had happened that spring: no battle, no treaty, no royal visit. It stays near zero on function words and punctuation, on everyday domestic and modern-institutional vocabulary (kettle, towel, ladder, table, chair, house, kitchen, boat, money, bread, phone, office, committee, database), on the common core of ordinary adjectives and verbs (big, enormous, prodigious, announced, walked), on administrative or technical jargon used in its technical sense (parliament, ministry, legislation, jurisdiction, bureaucracy, software, browser, protocol), and on very obscure bookish words of the same register (frigate, vellum, edict, minstrel, abbey).
